title: This Essay is 10% AI Generated | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: Alex Danco argues that the '100% AI generated' Pangram dunk is not anti-AI sentiment but a social demand for authorship, reading LLM token prediction as a literal vindication of Barthes' 'death of the author' and LLM verbal tics (pushy qualifiers, forced synthesis) as fine-tuning backfilling Foucault's 'author-function' to compensate for authorlessness. Despite the title, the text discloses that 0% of the words were LLM-written — the '10%' refers to idea-level collaboration with a model called Sol 5.6 — and he flags that watermarking announcements and the Pangram-vs-evasion arms race may arrive exactly when reliable frontier detection is already closing.

themes.theme: Preference falsification in the market for AI prose

insights.claim: Public distaste for AI-generated writing is classic preference falsification, and the marketplace of writing will bend toward readers' revealed rather than stated preferences — implying AI prose gains share even while it remains socially scorned.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Bet on consumption data, not survey sentiment, when sizing markets for AI writing tools and AI-assisted media; stated backlash is a poor short signal.
insights.quote: AI writing has all the hallmarks of classic preference falsification.
insights.locator: “100% of this text is AI” is the new

insights.claim: Assuming AI will stay excellent at code and other practical output while remaining inferior at prose is presumptuous; the prose gap is more likely a temporary artifact than a durable moat for human writers.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Content and media businesses pricing in a permanent human-prose premium are exposed if the prose gap closes on the same curve as code.
insights.quote: It feels presumptuous to think that AI might be great at writing code and other kinds of practical output, but remain inferior in prose for much longer.
insights.locator: AI writing has all the hallmarks of classic

insights.claim: As of August 2026 an AI-native a16z editor still refuses to edit or publish AI-written prose because 'you can feel it' most of the time, indicating the detection edge currently sits with trained human readers rather than tools.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Editorial gatekeeping remains a human-labor cost center in AI-era publishing; automation of the editing layer lags automation of the drafting layer.
insights.quote: I don’t like editing or publishing stuff that’s AI-written. I still think that, for now, “you can feel it” a lot of the time.
insights.locator: But I have a confession to make

insights.claim: The people most frequently posting Pangram AI-detection scores as a dunk are mostly tech insiders rather than AI opponents, so the behavior signals demand for authorship, not anti-AI ideology.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: The AI-detection market's real customer is provenance and attribution, not AI suppression — build and invest accordingly.
insights.quote: Look at the people doing the pangram quoting; it’s mostly people in tech, not AI haters.
insights.locator: Dunking on something as AI-written is performing

insights.claim: Calling text out as AI-generated performs Foucault's 'author-function': it creates an authorship category used to classify, assign meta-significance to, and police discourse, independent of whether the underlying text is good.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Provenance labels will function as a regulatory and reputational layer over content, not merely a quality filter — a distinct product surface from model quality.
insights.quote: The function of an author is to characterize the existence, circulation, and operation of certain discourses in society.
insights.locator: For Foucault, even if words have meaning independently

insights.claim: The AI-authorship debate is a replay of the 1967-1969 Barthes-Foucault sequence: Barthes unbundled authorship from meaning and Foucault re-bundled it as a social indexing function, with 'AI-generated' now serving as the new bundle.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Expect a durable market for authorship-classification infrastructure rather than a transient moral panic that fades with AI adoption.
insights.quote: Barthes unbundled authorship, Foucault made the new bundle.
insights.locator: So, Barthes and Foucault’s back and forth here

insights.claim: When literal authorship is unknown, societies historically invent indexing substitutes such as 'Pseudo-Aristotle' or the composite 'Homer', implying AI-era content will get analogous synthetic author labels rather than no labels at all.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Model-name-as-byline ('written with Claude', 'a Sol 5.6 piece') is the likely equilibrium; brand attaches to the model, creating a consumer-facing moat for model companies.
insights.quote: If we don’t have authorship handy as a meaning-compressor, we need to come up with some indexing substitute.
insights.locator: He’s saying, look: all of this writing is useless

themes.theme: Token prediction as detectable prose signature

insights.claim: A reliable LLM tell is inverted-emphasis phrasing — a model writes 'Give the pruning logic real attention' where a human writes 'Pay attention to the pruning logic' — a construction readers flag as alien even when the sentence is coherent.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Detection heuristics that key on syntactic entry-point statistics, not vocabulary, are the harder-to-evade layer of the detection stack.
insights.quote: A human would write, “Pay attention to the pruning logic”, whereas Claude here has produced, “Give the pruning logic real attention”
insights.locator: Give the prune logic real attention

insights.claim: The mechanism behind LLM style tells is that token prediction optimizes for reaching a sound destination while keeping options open word by word, biasing sentences toward statistically likely, low-commitment openings.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Style tells are architectural, not stylistic, so RLHF-era 'write more human' prompting is a shallow fix; real evasion requires decoding-level changes.
insights.quote: The LLM is optimizing for ultimately arriving at a sound destination, but it’s doing so in a way that keeps its options open, word by word.
insights.locator: My hunch here (and this isn’t an original thought

insights.claim: Humans compose by iterating through several sentence variants before committing, whereas LLMs proceed continuously from statistically likely entry points — a process difference, not a knowledge difference, that produces the residual detectability of AI prose.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Products that give models a draft-and-revise loop (rather than single-pass generation) attack the last visible quality gap in AI writing.
insights.quote: I’m working through a few different sentence variants before starting to write it out, whereas the LLM is approaching the chain of thought continuously, starting from statistically likely entry points.
insights.locator: Humans don’t exactly write like this

insights.claim: Barthes' 1967 claim that a word arrives pre-loaded with meaning that constrains the next word is a literal description of how LLMs generate text, making LLMs an unintended empirical vindication of the death-of-the-author thesis.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: A useful frame for arguing that AI writing is a difference of degree, not kind, from human writing — the ground on which copyright and authorship fights will be argued.
insights.quote: This is, straightforwardly, how LLMs are doing their thing.
insights.locator: This is very much Barthes’ music here

insights.claim: Danco scores Barthes as roughly 95% correct on the death of the author, since the only surviving human distinctive is that a person would construct the same meaning in a slightly different sequence.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: If only ~5% of authorship is human-distinctive, pricing power in written content shifts toward distribution and identity rather than the writing itself.
insights.quote: he’s still probably 95% on-the-money here, if the best argument we can make against it is, “well, if a human did it, it’d construct the meaning in a slightly different sequence.”
insights.locator: LLMs, therefore, should be a total and complete triumph

themes.theme: Synthetic author-function as a fine-tuning artifact

insights.claim: Asked how two ideas relate, models are systematically over-confident that the ideas are deeply connected and eager to collapse a conversation into 'one big idea' — a consistent failure mode of AI-assisted synthesis.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Anyone using LLMs for research synthesis should treat asserted connections as unverified priors; false-connection rate is the key eval metric for AI research tools.
insights.quote: Whenever I ask AI “What’s the relationship between these two ideas”, it tends to be suspiciously confident that the two ideas are deeply, emphatically related.
insights.locator: Whenever I ask AI “What’s the relationship

insights.claim: Danco's hypothesis is that LLM verbal tics — unnecessary qualifiers, humblebrags, forced logical groupings resolving into lines like 'that’s the quiet brilliance of it' — are fine-tuning backfilling a synthetic author-function to compensate for the model's authorlessness.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: If the annoying tics are RLHF-induced rather than architectural, they are removable — a fixable product problem separating model labs that solve tone from those that do not.
insights.quote: The writing style is optimizing for the creation of author-function.
insights.locator: Perhaps LLMs, having onboarded onto a semi-complete scope

insights.claim: Because readers demand an author, models are effectively forced to manufacture one in their prose — Danco's Voltaire inversion: if a wise and brilliant author does not exist, the LLM has to invent one.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Model persona is not cosmetic; it is a structural requirement of readable output and therefore a real differentiator between consumer AI products.
insights.quote: To bastardize Voltaire, if a wise and brilliant author doesn’t exist, the LLM has to invent one.
insights.locator: All of the totally “unnecessary” qualifiers and humblebrags

themes.theme: Watermarking, false positives, and the detection arms race

insights.claim: In the weeks before mid-August 2026 there was a flurry of announcements from model companies and other AI ecosystem players committing to watermark outputs for easy AI detection, a shift Danco calls overdue rather than surprising.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Watermarking is becoming table stakes; provenance tooling and compliance vendors get a demand tailwind, while pure detection-only vendors face substitution.
insights.quote: we’ve gotten this flurry of announcements from model companies and other AI ecosystem players about how they’re going to be watermarking outputs for easy AI detection. I’m frankly surprised it took this long.
insights.locator: In the past few weeks, we’ve gotten this flurry

insights.claim: Detection has become an explicit arms race between Pangram improving detection and models improving evasion, and Danco suspects the window of reliable AI detection at the frontier may already be closed.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Standalone AI-detection businesses face a shrinking moat; value migrates to source-side watermarking and cryptographic provenance where the model owner controls the signal.
insights.quote: There’s no question that we’re now in an arms race between “Can Pangram get better at detecting” and “can AI get better at avoiding”
insights.locator: It could be, as often occurs historically

insights.claim: The peak of public reaction to AI detection may historically coincide with the moment the thing being reacted to stops mattering — the watermarking wave could be arriving precisely as detection loses efficacy.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: A general timing heuristic: maximum discourse volume is a contrarian signal that the underlying dynamic is already resolving.
insights.quote: It could be, as often occurs historically, that the peak reaction to the thing is the moment when the thing stops mattering.
insights.locator: In the past few weeks, we’ve gotten this flurry

insights.claim: Pangram scored several of Danco's own human-written 2019-2020 blog posts at 70-75% AI Generated, a concrete false-positive demonstration that undercuts using detection scores as evidence.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Detection-score reputational attacks are unreliable enough to carry legal and PR risk for platforms that act on them; a real opening for provenance-at-source alternatives.
insights.quote: Last week I went back and ran Pangram through some of my 2019-2020 era blog posts, just out of curiosity. Several of them threw scores of “70-75% AI Generated”.
insights.locator: Authorship is a thing that people value

themes.theme: Authorship as the scarce asset and disclosure norms

insights.claim: Demand for authorship persists because authorship is itself meaning — the indexing, relation, and handling of ideas is what makes an idea legible — so provenance, not prose quality, is what becomes scarce as generation costs go to zero.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: The defensible layer in AI-era media is identity, curation, and index — not word production; value accrues to bylines and taste, not to volume.
insights.quote: They want authorship because it is meaning, because the indexing and relation and handling of ideas is itself the meaning of the idea.
insights.locator: Still, I am occasionally a believer in the wisdom of crowds

insights.claim: Despite a headline claiming the piece is 10% AI generated, the text discloses that 0% of its words came from an LLM; the 10% figure prices idea-level iteration with a model called Sol 5.6, proposing a disclosure norm based on contribution to thinking rather than to text.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: AI-contribution disclosure will need to measure ideation as well as generation; watermarking of tokens misses the dominant real-world use of AI as a thinking partner.
insights.quote: None of the words here came from an LLM; I typed them all with my hands. I did talk to Sol 5.6 a fair bit, though, to iterate through some of the ideas. So 10% authorship seemed fair.
insights.locator: I should mention, in closing

insights.claim: Danco reads high AI-detection scores on his own pre-LLM writing as possible evidence that models were trained on his corpus, treating training-data influence as a plausible cause of stylistic convergence rather than coincidence.
insights.speaker: Alex Danco
insights.so_what: Style-convergence-as-training-evidence is a live argument thread for content licensing and copyright disputes with model labs.
insights.quote: Maybe it means the AI was actually trained on me! I’d be honored.
insights.locator: Authorship is a thing that people value
